topic: Japan moves closer to letting US nuclear weapons into the country, breaking a 55-year principle

sources.title: Takaichi keeps future anti-nuke policy vague in Hiroshima
sources.text:
THE ASAHI SHIMBUN
August 7, 2026 at 17:43 JST
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, left, speaks at a meeting to hear atomic bomb survivors’ comments in Hiroshima on Aug. 6. (Toshiyuki Hayashi)
HIROSHIMA--Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stopped short of ruling out future revisions to Japan’s non-nuclear weapons policy during her visit here for the Aug. 6 peace memorial ceremony, choosing to leave her intentions unclear.
Attention had focused ahead of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony on how Takaichi would address Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles in front of atomic bomb survivors and bereaved families.
Hiroshima was one of only two cities in the world devastated by an atomic bomb in 1945.
The issue drew particular interest because Takaichi had previously argued that the principle prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan was “unrealistic.”
That signaled a willingness to revise that part of the long-standing policy established in line with the nation’s pacifist Constitution.
In her speech at the annual ceremony on Aug. 6, Takaichi said, “Our country firmly upholds the Three Non-Nuclear Principles.”
After the memorial, however, when asked by reporters about a possible revision of the three security-related documents, which is scheduled for the end of this year, she declined to comment.
As global momentum toward nuclear disarmament continues to recede, a representative of hibakusha put a direct question to the prime minister: “Will the Three Non-Nuclear Principles be revised?”
Under the blazing morning sun, Takaichi attended the ceremony for the first time since taking office in October.
Addressing approximately 50,000 attendees, including atomic bomb survivors and bereaved family members, she said, “Our country firmly upholds the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, and as the only country to have suffered atomic bombings in war, we have a mission to tirelessly continue our efforts toward achieving a world without nuclear weapons.”
After the ceremony, Takaichi spent about 30 minutes touring the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, and viewed children’s belongings caught up in the blast, including a tricycle and a charred lunch box.
According to museum director Yoshifumi Ishida, Takaichi said, “The devastating reality of the atomic bombing has left a profound impression on me” and wrote the words “Pray for peace” in the museum’s guest book.
A-BOMB SURVIVORS POSE QUESTION TO TAKAICHI
The prime minister then attended a meeting at a hotel in Hiroshima with representatives of seven local atomic bomb survivors’ organizations to hear their requests.
Among those present was Satoshi Tanaka, 82, secretary-general of Liaison Conference of Hiroshima Hibakusha Organizations, who had come directly from the hospital where he was hospitalized.
Tanaka entered Hiroshima after the bombing and was exposed to radiation when he was 17 months old.
For decades, he has campaigned for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
He said he wanted to confirm whether Takaichi intended to uphold indefinitely the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, the longstanding national policy under which Japan neither possesses nor manufactures nuclear weapons and does not permit their introduction into the country.
Before becoming prime minister, Takaichi argued in a 2024 publication she co-authored that the “do not permit the introduction” component of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles should be reconsidered, describing it as “unrealistic” given Japan’s reliance on the U.S. nuclear umbrella.
At the meeting, Tanaka posed a question directly to her.
“The world today stands at a crossroads between moving toward nuclear war and continuing along the path of peace. Will the Three Non-Nuclear Principles be revised?”
“Japan upholds the Three Non-Nuclear Principles,” Takaichi replied.
However, she did not say that she will not revise them in the future.
After the meeting, Tanaka said, “‘Japan upholds’ is merely a description of the current situation. I did not see any determination not to revise them.”
Kunihiko Sakuma, 81, who heads the Hiroshima Council of A-bomb Sufferers Organizations, voiced a similar concern, saying, “She did not address what she intends to do in the future. It sounded like a stopgap answer,” he said.
Another survivor also referred to Takaichi’s visit to the museum.
Hiroshi Harada, 87, chairman of the Hiroshima Prefectural Confederation of A-bomb Sufferers Organizations, another organization representing atomic bomb survivors, and a former director of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, was 6 when he was exposed to the atomic bombing near Hiroshima Station.
“The exhibits you saw today are far too limited compared with what we actually experienced,” he told Takaichi. “I hope you do not think that they fully convey the devastation caused by the atomic bomb.”
Harada later said he made the comment because he had long questioned whether Takaichi truly understood the inhumane nature of nuclear weapons.
At a news conference after the meeting, Takaichi declined to comment when asked by reporters on the potential revision of Japan’s three security-related documents, a process that could involve changing the Three Non-Nuclear Principles.
“I would like to refrain from making any assumptions at this stage about the wording or other aspects” of the revision, she said.
At a separate news conference on Aug. 6, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara was questioned about Takaichi’s reference to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles.
Reporters noted that her recent speeches had indicated future policy direction, whereas her remarks this time appeared to describe only the current situation.
Kihara only said, “The government upholds the Three Non-Nuclear Principles as a matter of policy, and the prime minister’s remarks were made on the basis of that position.”
Since taking office, Takaichi has largely set aside her personal views. She has repeatedly said in the Diet that “The government upholds the Three Non-Nuclear Principles,” when responding to questions.
The administration has also maintained the position taken in 2010 by then Foreign Minister Katsuya Okada, who argued that if Japan’s security required allowing visits by U.S. vessels carrying nuclear weapons, the government of the day would make that decision and explain it to the public.
PRO-NUKE TAKAICHI ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS
Meanwhile, pro-nuclear remarks continue to flow from within the Takaichi administration.
In December 2025, a senior official at the Prime Minister’s Office told reporters, while stressing that it was a personal opinion, that Japan should possess nuclear weapons.
In July, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said on an internet program that discussion of nuclear weapons was unavoidable.
Referring to Europe’s efforts to strengthen its nuclear deterrent, he argued that Japan must “debate and pursue all policy options without taboos.”
Nippon Ishin (Japan Innovation Party), which joined the ruling coalition after Takaichi became prime minister in October, has also pushed for a review of the country’s anti-nuclear policy.
Ahead of revisions to the three security-related documents, the party recommended the government review the principle of prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan, calling for a “realistic examination.”
Whether Takaichi’s repeated use of the phrase “Japan upholds the three principles” in Hiroshima constituted a guarantee for the future or merely a description of the present remains unclear.
Without providing a definitive answer to Hiroshima hibakusha, she is scheduled to meet with atomic bomb survivors again in Nagasaki on Aug. 9, when the Nagasaki Peace Memorial Ceremony is held.
(This article was written by Hajimu Takeda, Takahiro Kinomura and Suzuka Tominaga.)

sources.title: Japan moves closer to letting nuclear weapons into the country
sources.text:
THE ASAHI SHIMBUN
November 12, 2026 at 15:14 JST
The Takaichi administration is pushing ahead with plans to create an exception to one of Japan’s three principles concerning nuclear weapons, but the move is facing resistance within the ruling party.
A senior government official said Nov. 11 the administration intends to allow nuclear weapons into Japan in certain emergency situations, and include that exception in three key national security documents due for revision by year-end.
Specifically, the exception could allow U.S. nuclear-armed ships to make emergency port calls in Japan if the government determines that Japan could not otherwise be adequately defended.
“It will naturally be a subject for discussion,” the official said.
The Three Non-Nuclear Principles commit Japan to not possess, produce or permit nuclear weapons to be brought into the country.
The current security documents say Japan’s policy of adhering to the principles “will remain unchanged.”
Although successive governments since 2010 have maintained that an exception could be made to defend Japan, but it has never been explicitly written into the security documents.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the principle of not allowing nuclear weapons into Japan “unrealistic,” given Japan’s reliance on U.S. extended nuclear deterrence.
RESISTANCE INSIDE RULING BLOC
But the plan to formally spell out an exception has been opposed within Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party.
“If we put an exception explicitly in writing, it will no longer be an exception,” said a former defense minister from the LDP. “It would only create unnecessary friction with neighboring countries and further worsen Japan’s diplomatic environment.”
However, the LDP’s coalition partner, Nippon Ishin (Japan Innovation Party), has called for “realistic consideration” of the principle of not allowing nuclear weapons into Japan, citing possible future visits by U.S. nuclear submarines carrying nuclear-armed cruise missiles.
The ruling parties began talks on revising the security documents on Nov. 10.
Terumi Tanaka, 94, a representative of Nihon Hidankyo (Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers Organizations), criticized the move.
“What will happen once they start tampering with the principle of ‘not permitting nuclear weapons to be brought into Japan’?” Tanaka said. “They don’t understand the horrors of nuclear weapons.”
Tanaka said Nihon Hidankyo has long called for the principles to be enshrined in law rather than left to successive governments to change.
He also said a major nationwide movement is needed to push Japan toward joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

sources.title: Japan to go nuclear? Russia warns Tokyo could get nukes within a year
sources.text:
Amid Japan's ongoing push for remilitarization, Russia has warned that Tokyo could develop its own nuclear weapons within a year. According to Russia's TASS news agency, Anton Kobyakov, Russian Presidential Assistant and Executive Secretary of the Organising Committee of the Eastern Economic Forum, said Japan could possess nuclear weapons within one year.
"There is even talk about nuclear weapons, which Japan is capable of assembling in about a year. Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi’s aggressive rhetoric shows that the country’s former role in the broader framework of US regional and global strategy has changed significantly, shifting towards direct involvement," he was quoted as saying by TASS.
At a memorial service marking the 81st anniversary of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima in early August, Takaichi said Japan still follows its three non-nuclear principles. However, she did not make a clear commitment that the principles would continue to be maintained in the future.
China also raises Japan's nuclear potential
Earlier this month, China also renewed its warnings about Japan's nuclear potential. Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui claimed that Tokyo has enough plutonium to theoretically produce thousands of nuclear warheads.
In an article published by TASS, Zhang said Japan had 44.4 tonnes of plutonium extracted from spent nuclear fuel as of the end of 2024. He claimed the stockpile could be used to manufacture around 5,500 nuclear warheads.
Trending Stories
The ambassador also said Japan's spent nuclear fuel storage facilities contained another 191 tonnes of unextracted plutonium.
The statements come as Tokyo pushes to remilitarize the country amid rising tensions in its neighbourhood with China and North Korea. Geopolitical uncertainty and US President Donald Trump's changing stance towards allies have also prompted Washington's partners to increase defence spending.
Japan-Russia tensions deepen
Relations between Russia and Japan have also come under strain following the war in Ukraine. Tensions increased further after Russian President Vladimir Putin recently visited the Kuril Islands for the first time, prompting strong protests from Tokyo, which also claims the territory.
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin on one of the four main Kuril Islands. Russian media reported that he visited a fish processing plant and was presented with caviar.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi criticised Putin's visit and said it "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable."
"The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law," Takaichi told reporters. She added that the visit "made it more difficult to restore relations in the medium to long term."
Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolai Nozdrev on Thursday to lodge a "strong protest" over Putin's visit.
Motegi told the ambassador that Putin's visit would "have an extremely negative impact on Japan-Russia relations", according to a statement from the ministry.
Relations between the two countries have already faced pressure following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

sources.title: Chinese FM slams Japan’s growing nuclear ambitions after Takaichi hints at exceptions to non-nuclear principles
sources.text:
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning
Relevant remarks once again exposed the Japanese authorities' growing nuclear ambitions, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Friday, responding to remarks by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at a House of Representatives Budget Committee session on October 14. Takaichi claimed there was "still room for discussion" over former foreign minister Katsuya Okada's suggestion that, under exceptional circumstances, US forces could be allowed to bring nuclear weapons into Japan, implying possible exceptions to Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles.
Japan's current government is disregarding its international non-proliferation obligations and seeking a gradual "loosening of nuclear restraints" by strengthening extended deterrence arrangements with allies, seeking to abandon the Three Non-Nuclear Principles, introducing nuclear-powered submarines and even pursuing the deployment of nuclear weapons in Japan, Mao said. Such moves would seriously threaten peace and stability in Asia and beyond, Mao said.
The reporter also noted that, in response to a proposal by the Japan Innovation Party to introduce nuclear-powered submarines, Takaichi claimed Japan would conduct concrete and realistic discussions.
Mao stressed that there was no room for "discussion" when it comes to upholding the postwar international order and fulfilling international obligations. She urged Japan to face the concerns of the international community, deeply reflect on the historical crimes of Japanese militarism, completely abandon attempts at "remilitarization" and nuclear armament, and avoid once again placing itself in opposition to the international community.
Also on Friday, Mao was also asked to comment on Japan's discussions over introducing nuclear-powered submarines, and about remarks by Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, who claimed Japan possesses neither nuclear weapons nor strategic bombers, while China has both and yet criticizes Japan.
Mao said Japan was a defeated country in World War II and a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Japan must not breach its exclusively defense-oriented policy and must not possess nuclear weapons, as these are obligations under international law.
"On issues of history and law, Japanese politicians need to brush up on their lessons," Mao said.

sources.title: Japan mulls exception to non-nuclear principles in security strategy
sources.text:
Japan mulls exception to non-nuclear principles in security strategy
(Mainichi Japan)
TOKYO (Kyodo) -- The Japanese government is considering explicitly stating an exception to its long-standing non-nuclear principles in an updated security strategy, a source familiar with the matter said Thursday, apparently aiming to enhance the effectiveness of U.S. nuclear deterrence protecting Japan.
One option under consideration is to state in the document that Japan would allow nuclear weapons to be brought into the country in an emergency, reflecting a position outlined by a foreign minister in parliament in 2010 and endorsed by successive governments, including that of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
The three principles, upheld by Japan as the only country to have suffered nuclear attacks, prohibit the possession, production or introduction of nuclear weapons.
Before becoming prime minister, Takaichi, known as a security hawk, expressed doubts about the principle of not allowing nuclear weapons into Japan, which could complicate port calls by nuclear-armed U.S. vessels and weaken the credibility of U.S. nuclear deterrence in a contingency.
While likely stopping short of revising the three principles themselves, the government is leaning toward explicitly stating an exception to them in the National Security Strategy, which is to be updated along with other related documents by the end of the year.
Stating the exception in an official government document would likely signal a stronger commitment than remarks made in parliament. In that case, the government would also have to establish criteria for allowing nuclear weapons into Japan and procedures for decision-making by both the Japanese and U.S. governments.
The move could also fuel Chinese accusations of Japanese "neo-militarism" amid Takaichi's push to bolster the country's defense capabilities.
The exception to the three non-nuclear principles was raised in March 2010 by then Foreign Minister Katsuya Okada during a parliamentary committee session when the now-defunct Democratic Party of Japan was in power.
"If Japan's safety cannot be guaranteed without allowing a temporary port call by a U.S. vessel carrying nuclear weapons, the government should stake its fate and make a decision, and explain it to the public," he said.
The three non-nuclear principles came under intense scrutiny more than a decade ago when a Japanese Foreign Ministry panel acknowledged the existence of a secret Cold War-era pact under which Tokyo allowed nuclear-armed U.S. vessels to visit Japanese ports without the required prior consultation. Okada led the investigation that uncovered the pact.
After taking office in October last year, Takaichi initially said she shared Okada's view on the exception. But she appeared to shift her position last month, telling a parliamentary committee that there was "room for consideration" regarding how the upcoming security documents should address U.S. extended deterrence and Okada's remarks.
Extended deterrence refers to the U.S. commitment to use its full range of nuclear and conventional capabilities to defend Japan, which faces an increasingly challenging security environment amid China's growing military assertiveness and North Korea's nuclear and missile threats.
Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said in October that the government needed to consider how other countries might perceive the move if Japan explicitly included Okada's remarks in the security documents.
The actual wording may become a key issue in working-level consultations between the Liberal Democratic Party, some of whose members are wary of revising the three principles, and its junior coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party, which is more supportive of a change.
Leaving the three principles unchanged while referring to Okada's remarks as an exception in the security documents could provide a compromise, the source said.
In the current National Security Strategy, adopted in 2022, the government pledged to maintain an exclusively defense-oriented policy, refrain from becoming a military power that poses a threat to other countries and uphold the three non-nuclear principles.

sources.title: Takaichi weighs exception to Japan's nonnuclear policy amid security shifts
sources.text:
Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on the 14th that there is "room to consider" past remarks by a Japanese cabinet minister that could be interpreted as allowing an exception to bringing in nuclear weapons under the national policy of maintaining the "three non-nuclear principles." The comment draws attention because it leaves open the possibility of revising the three non-nuclear principles, whose core is "not possessing, not producing, and not bringing in nuclear weapons."
At the House of Representatives Budget Committee in the Diet that day, Prime Minister Takaichi was asked about the three non-nuclear principles and replied that there is room to consider remarks made in 2010, when the Democratic Party was in power, by then-Foreign Minister Katsuya Okada.
At the time, former Foreign Minister Okada answered in the Diet that, assuming a situation in which Japan could not protect its security without recognizing port calls by U.S. nuclear-armed vessels, "the administration must stake its fate, make a decision, and explain it to the public." This meant the administration should decide to allow U.S. nuclear-armed vessels to call at Japanese ports in emergencies such as war for national security, a position that conflicts with the clause of the three non-nuclear principles that bans bringing into Japan nuclear weapons made by other countries.
Before taking office, Prime Minister Takaichi had shown a critical stance toward the principle of banning the bringing in of nuclear weapons. In the book "Study of national power," published just before last year's Liberal Democratic Party leadership election, Takaichi argued, "Even if we continue to adhere to the bans on possession and production (of nuclear weapons), it is not realistic to 'not bring them in' if we expect U.S. extended deterrence."
Japan Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi backed Takaichi's remarks in the Diet the same day, saying, "Compared with the time when former Foreign Minister Okada answered, the severity (of the situation) has increased overwhelmingly, and the various forms of threats are also expanding." Motegi added, "While we maintain the three non-nuclear principles, there is a need to consider them based on the greatly changed security environment and threat perception within that framework."
However, in her Diet response that day, Takaichi refrained from further comment on specific language related to the three non-nuclear principles in the three key security documents the cabinet is moving to revise within the year with a focus on boosting national defense capabilities, saying, "I will refrain from presuming." She also repeated the position she gave in the Diet on the 7th regarding "nuclear sharing," which would deploy U.S. nuclear weapons in Japan for joint operation, saying, "Nuclear sharing is not currently being considered in Japan, and it is not appropriate."
The Asahi Shimbun reported that within the government, a plan is emerging to maintain the three non-nuclear principles in the three key security documents while additionally specifying former Foreign Minister Okada's answer. The outlet projected that nuclear submarines carrying the sea-launched nuclear cruise missile (SLCM-N), which the U.S. government decided to develop in 2018 during the first Donald Trump administration, could call at Japanese ports sometime in the 2030s.
